entire review — Run a multi-agent review against a branch
Run a multi-agent review against the current branch or a --target branch:
several reviewer agents review the change in parallel, then a single judge consolidates their
reports into the final verdict in a closing round. Reviews are saved as named
profiles in Entire settings and clone-local preferences. On first run, guided
setup writes a profile and asks before starting agents.

Flags:
  --configure    set up a review profile (shows available agents + profiles).
                 With --set-* flags it writes the profile non-interactively;
                 otherwise it opens the wizard (interactive) without starting agents.
  --set-agents   with --configure: comma-separated reviewer agents for the profile
  --set-judge    with --configure: the consolidating judge as agent[=model]
  --set-output   with --configure: where the verdict goes: local (default) or trail
  --local        with --configure: save to .entire/settings.local.json (just you)
                 instead of .entire/settings.json (shared). Interactive setup asks.
  --set-task     with --configure: the profile's canonical task text
  --set-model    with --configure: per-reviewer model as agent=model (repeatable)
  --set-slot     with --configure: a reviewer slot as agent[=model] (repeatable;
                 the same agent/model may repeat to run it multiple times)
  --set-config   with --configure: a reviewer's own agent config as
                 reviewer=<config.json|isolated|none> (repeatable). It replaces
                 the reviewed checkout's hooks, MCP servers and extensions; the
                 checkout's skills still load. Saved to clone-local preferences.
  --edit         re-open the advanced profile skill picker
  --findings     browse local findings; pass a handle to print one saved run
  --agent NAME   run only one reviewer from the selected profile
  --list         list configured review profiles (their reviewers and judge)
  --agents       list the reviewer agents you can pass to --agent for the profile
  --model NAME   override the model for the --agent reviewer (requires --agent)
  --models       list the models each agent advertises (optionally --agent NAME)
  --profile NAME select a profile (also accepted as positional arg)
  --prompt TEXT  add one-off per-run instructions for this invocation
  --timeout DUR  optional hard cap on each reviewer before it's cancelled and
                 marked failed. No default — reviewers run until they finish,
                 like a directly-invoked skill. A positive value also bounds
                 the consolidating judge, which otherwise keeps its own 20m
                 default (the judge is never unbounded; its timeout or error
                 fails the review with no verdict). A timed-out reviewer's
                 siblings and the judge still proceed.
  --base REF     scope against REF instead of mainline. Useful for stacked
                 PRs where the base is the parent feature branch, not main.
                 Default: first existing of origin/HEAD, origin/main,
                 origin/master, main, master.
  --target REF   check out a branch identified by branch name, trail ID, or
                 Entire trail URL in a worktree and run the review there.
  --cleanup-worktree
                 remove a newly-created target worktree after a successful
                 review. Interactive runs ask when this flag is omitted.
  --show-config  list what the review would run (hooks, MCP servers, settings)
                 and exit without checking anything out. Add --json for
                 structured output.
  --trust-target SHA
                 approve reviewing code by someone else at this commit. Reviews
                 of commits you did not author need approval because the
                 reviewer loads the checkout's hooks, MCP servers, and settings.

To tag an already-finished session as a review, use
'entire session attach --review <id>'.

entire api — Make an authenticated request to an Entire API and print the response
Make an authenticated HTTP request to an Entire API and print the JSON response.

These endpoints are internal and can change shape without notice; where a
purpose-built command exists, its output is the stable interface.

The CLI attaches the right bearer token and dials the right host for the
chosen backend, so you don't have to plumb auth yourself:

  --to core   the control plane (default): orgs, repos, mirrors, clusters, /me
  --to cell   your home entire-api cell: /me/* activity, repo aggregates

Use --jurisdiction <slug> (e.g. us, eu) to reach a specific jurisdiction's
entire-api cell instead of your home one; it implies --to cell.

Both backends act as ENTIRE_TOKEN when set, else the selected login
(--context, else $ENTIRE_CONTEXT, else the active context), so a staging
login reaches staging's control plane and cells. The cell host comes from
environment's cluster listing; an explicit ENTIRE_API_BASE_URL names the
data host directly instead.

<path> is the full path on that host, e.g. /api/v1/clusters. These
placeholders are filled from the current repo's origin remote:
  {owner} {repo}   the GitHub owner / repo
  {repo_id}        the repo's Entire ULID (from its mirror) — cells key on this

The method is GET unless a field/body is given (then POST); override with -X.

When to use this:
LAST RESORT. Right in two cases: you are developing against Entire's own
APIs and want a raw response, or no first-class command covers your need.
Otherwise prefer the command built for the job (checkpoint, session, trail,
status, repo, …) — its output is stable, raw endpoints are not. If you are
reaching for this during ordinary work in a repo with Entire enabled, run
`entire agent-help` first; there is probably a command for it. When you do
need it, use this rather than hand-rolling curl — it attaches the right
bearer and dials the right host for you.

- **Build:** `go vet` and the unit tests pass for `agents/entire-agent-sarvam` at `d871a4e`.

The slop half is done and I've spot-checked it. The adversarial bug hunt is still running, so this covers only the slop gate.

## Slop gate: Medium is justified

I re-ran the gate's exact prompt from `.entire/runners/trail-slop.json` on the final diff and got Medium again. The two strongest reasons:

1. **`config.go` is a 603-line hand-written TOML editor, and no test checks that its output is valid TOML.** Hermes does the same job in 172 lines by using a YAML library. Editing line by line is defensible here, because Go has no TOML library that keeps comments when it writes. But this file goes well past install and uninstall:
   - It tracks multi-line strings and arrays (`parseConfigBlocks`, `netBracketsOutsideQuotes`).
   - It repairs the user's own malformed hooks (`repairParentlessHooks`) and rejects table-form hooks (`checkNoMapFormEvents`).
   - It has its own string escaping and unescaping.

   The 689-line `config_test.go` only checks that certain text appears in the output, so nothing proves Sarvam can actually load the file it writes.
2. **Too many comments.** About 17% of the added non-test lines in `internal/sarvam` are comments. Many are paragraph-length, describe past versions of the code, or are now wrong.

## What should bring it down to Low, in priority order

1. **`config_test.go`:** parse every config the tests write with a real TOML parser (for example `BurntSushi/toml` as a test-only dependency). Assert that `hooks.<Event>` is a list of groups containing our command.
2. **`config.go`:** cut it back to "add or remove our own blocks".

content.text:
The adversarial review is done. It found two medium bugs, both in `config.go`, the hand-written TOML editor that the slop gate already flagged. For both, the reviewer ran install → check → second install → uninstall in a throwaway test and checked each output with Python's TOML parser. I re-read the code behind the first one, and it does count raw `"""` on the whole line.

## Medium

1. **A `"""` or `'''` in a comment or ordinary string hides every hook below it** (`config.go:154-158`). The check that starts a multi-line string counts the delimiter anywhere on the line, comments and quoted strings included. A user line such as `# wrap long prompts in """` or `notify = "echo '''"` causes this:
   - `AreHooksInstalled` returns false after a successful install.
   - Each re-install adds 4 more Entire hooks, so they fire more than once.
   - Uninstall removes none of them.

   `netBracketsOutsideQuotes` a few lines above already skips quotes and `#`. This check needs the same handling.
2. **Install produces invalid TOML when the user defines hooks inline** (`config.go:363-383`, `:458`). `checkNoMapFormEvents` only rejects the `[hooks.<Event>]` header form. It misses `[hooks]` followed by `Stop = [{ hooks = [...] }]`, and a top-level `hooks.Stop = [...]`. In those cases install appends `[[hooks.Stop]]`, and the TOML parser rejects the file ("Cannot mutate immutable namespace"). Install still reports success, but Sarvam can't load the config, so all hooks stop working, including the user's own.

## Low

3. Valid header spellings like `[[ hooks.Stop ]]` or `[[hooks."Stop".hooks]]` aren't recognised, so install adds a duplicate and uninstall leaves the original behind (`config.go:65`).
4. On a CRLF file, new and rewritten lines are written with LF only, giving mixed line endings. It still parses (`config.go:317-321`, `:440`).
5. Extracting changed files from shell commands is a guess (`transcript.go:205-208`):
   - `git commit -m "fix: x > y"` reports a file named `y`.
   - `&> build.log`, `cp a b` and `rm old.txt` are missed.
   - Paths outside the repo, like `/tmp/x`, are returned too.
6. The e2e adapter's `trustRepo` runs a real, paid `sarvam-code exec` before every prompt, so each prompt makes two model calls (`e2e/agents/sarvam.go:209-228`). It also assumes Entire's hooks are the first group and first entry for each event (line 283), which holds only in a fresh test repo.
7. `testdata/hook-payloads/*.json` and `AGENT.md:23` contain `/Users/soph/...` paths. `AGENT.md:173` also describes tool-event hooks that are never installed.

## Checked and fine

The reviewer also confirmed these work:
- Transcript lines over 64 KB and a partial last line are read correctly.
- Token counts aren't double-counted.
- The exec-result fix (a failed command with empty output now reports an error) holds.
- The protocol dispatch matches qwen's.
- `write-session` won't overwrite an existing transcript.
- The repo-root `.sarvam/config.toml` follows the same pattern as the other agent configs committed here.

## Bottom line

Both medium bugs come from parsing TOML by hand. The fix the slop review suggested would close both: read and validate the file with a real TOML parser, keep hand edits only for writing, and make the tests parse what they write. That should also be the biggest step toward a Low slop rating. The cleanup items from the slop review (unused `EntryName`/`EventType` fields, stale comments, trimming the long comments) still apply.

Nothing has been posted to the trail. I can file the two medium bugs plus whichever low ones you want as findings on https://entire.com/gh/entireio/-/trails/2906/changes/external-agents/8. The review worktree at `.worktrees/sarvam-review` is clean; I can remove it when you're done.

# transcript

Package `github.com/entireio/cli/transcript` converts native agent transcripts
into the Entire Transcript Format and reads that format into typed Go values.

The library is versioned with CLI releases. Its API and the format may change;
consumers should pin a version.

## Entire Transcript Format v1

The format has been called the "compact transcript" (CLI code, metadata key
`compact_transcript`) and the "unified transcript" (entire-api). All three names
refer to the same thing. Stored names are unchanged: the file is
`transcript.jsonl`, the metadata key is `compact_transcript`, and the line field
is `cli_version`.

One JSON object per line, each line terminated by `\n`.

| Field | Type | Required | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `v` | int | yes | Always `1`. |
| `type` | string | yes | `user` or `assistant`. |
| `agent` | string | no | The CLI agent registry name (`claude-code`, `codex`, `copilot-cli`, `cursor`, `factoryai-droid`, `opencode`, `pi`, `antigravity`); otherwise the agent type string, e.g. for external agents. An open set. |
| `cli_version` | string | no | Version of the producer that wrote the line. The name is historical. |
| `ts` | string | no | Source timestamp where available, normally RFC 3339. May be omitted or empty when the native transcript has no timestamp. The generic JSONL converter copies source timestamps verbatim, so a non-string value can occur; readers ignore it. |
| `id` | string | no | Assistant message ID. Streaming fragments with the same ID are merged into one line. The Codex item path writes the item ID on user lines too. |
| `model` | string | no | Assistant lines only. The model the source reports for this call, verbatim; omitted when it reports none. Never inferred from a session-wide default, and never a placeholder: a value the agent writes in place of a model (Claude Code's `<synthetic>` on API-error entries) is omitted. |
| `input_tokens` | int | no | Assistant lines only. Input not counted in the line's `cache_read_tokens` or `cache_write_tokens`; see below. |
| `output_tokens` | int | no | Assistant lines only; includes reasoning tokens when the source reports them as part of output. |
| `cache_read_tokens`, `cache_write_tokens` | int | no | Assistant lines only; per-call cached input read and total cached input written. Cache counts are separate from fresh `input_tokens`. |
| `cache_write_5m_tokens`, `cache_write_1h_tokens` | int | no | Assistant lines only; an optional breakdown of `cache_write_tokens`, emitted only when the source reports the split (even when a reported value is zero). Absence means unknown, not zero or all 5m. Do not add the split to the total when summing usage. |
| `reasoning_tokens` | int | no | Assistant lines only; subset of `output_tokens` when reported by the source, not additional output. |
| `content` | array of blocks, string, or `null` | yes | Normally an array. A string can appear when an assistant message's source content was a string. `null` can appear because the writer does not omit empty content. |

Usage and model fields are per call, never copied from a session aggregate. A zero omitted by JSON encoding does not assert that the source reported zero.

On every line, `input_tokens` excludes the tokens in that line's `cache_read_tokens` and `cache_write_tokens`, so adding them never double counts. The sum is the call's total input only on lines from a converter that writes the cache fields. Lines written before that carry no cache fields, and their `input_tokens` is one of two things:

- Fresh input only (Claude Code, and Pi except as below): the cached input is missing from the line, so the sum understates the call's input.
- Fresh plus cached input (Codex, and Pi on Google models before pi-ai subtracted cached tokens in March 2026): the total is right, but its cache share is unknown, so pricing it at the fresh-input rate overstates the cost.

Other agents' lines copy the native input count as the agent defines it. Only `agent` and the `cli_version` that wrote a line tell these cases apart; no field marks a line as old or new, and `model` in particular says nothing about how `input_tokens` was counted.

Converters fill only what the native transcript reports per call. Claude Code, Codex and Pi record per-call usage and model, and their converters write them (below). Copilot CLI has only a shutdown aggregate, Cursor is hook-only, and external plugins and Antigravity report usage out of band, so their lines do not get these fields. Native timestamps are preserved where present; a missing one stays empty rather than fabricated.

### Per-call usage

An assistant line can carry usage with empty content (`"content":[]` or `"content":null`, for example an aborted or thinking-only call): readers that render transcripts should skip it, and readers that count usage must keep it.

Claude Code (`Options.Agent` `claude-code`, and `NewClaudeAdapter`; Cursor and Droid keep legacy counts): streaming fragments of one message ID become one line carrying the whole usage row with the strictly highest `output_tokens` (earlier wins ties) and the model of the first fragment that reports one, skipping Claude Code's `<synthetic>` placeholder; `ts` is the last fragment's. The 5m/1h cache-write split is emitted only when both durations are reported. A message with no usage object on any fragment has no model or usage fields. User entries holding only tool results between fragments of one ID do not split the call: the later fragments become separate lines without usage, and the best row stays on the call's first line (the first with visible content, since a thinking-only message has no line), so a call's usage is counted once. Read per-call usage from the full converted transcript: in a checkpoint slice (`ConvertWithBoundary`), a usage row that arrives after a tool result goes to the call's first line, which can sit before the slice boundary.

Codex, `response_item` path (rollouts from Codex versions that do not record items): one assistant line per model call, made of the reasoning, message and tool-call items up to the `token_count` that closes it (real order: call, output, `token_count`; outputs attach to their call by `call_id`). Usage is the difference between consecutive cumulative `info.total_token_usage` snapshots, and `ts` is the closing snapshot's when present, otherwise the last item's. Fresh input is `input - cached` clamped at zero; Codex lines carry no cache-write fields. Repeated snapshots and snapshots missing the input, cached-input or output counter are ignored, `reasoning_tokens` needs both adjacent snapshots to report it, and a decrease in any counter stops usage on later lines. A call with usage but no text or tool calls (for example reasoning-only) emits `content: []`, so consumers may see empty assistant lines; a call with neither usage nor content is omitted. Without usable `total_token_usage` snapshots (flat per-event totals are not read), no `token_count` closes a call, so consecutive assistant items merge into one line until the next user line or tool output; with usable snapshots, a tool output does not end its call. After a counter decrease, total snapshots still close calls but carry no usage, starting with the call the decrease closes. With `StartLine`, the last line before the boundary is part of the slice when its tool output or closing snapshot arrives after it (a one-line head overlap, which can repeat that call's usage); a later output for any earlier call lands only on that call's earlier line.

Codex, item path (current rollouts; see Blocks): one line per item, not per call. A call is the items up to the `token_count` that closes it, and its usage is computed exactly as on the `response_item` path: the same snapshot differences, fresh input, cached reads and reasoning, the model from `turn_context`, repeated snapshots ignored, and a counter decrease stopping usage. The usage goes on the call's last assistant line, so the call's earlier lines carry none. A call with usage but no assistant line (reasoning only) gets a usage-only line with `"content":null` and no `id`, whose `ts` is the closing snapshot's; other lines keep their item's `ts`. A user message ends the open call. With `StartLine`, the skipped lines seed the usage baseline, and the last line before the boundary is part of the slice when its call's closing snapshot arrives after it (a one-line head overlap).

Pi, one native message per call (no fragments to merge): `model` is `message.model`, and Pi's `input` is used as `input_tokens` unchanged, since the backends that report cached tokens already exclude them from it (a backend that folds cache reads into `input` cannot be told apart per call). `cache_write_1h_tokens` is Pi's `cacheWrite1h` and `cache_write_5m_tokens` the rest of `cacheWrite` (clamped at 0 if 1h exceeds it), only when Pi reports `cacheWrite1h`. `reasoning_tokens` is Pi's `reasoning` when reported. An assistant message with no visible content but non-zero usage (thinking-only, aborted) gets a line with `"content":null` (`"content":[]` before Pi went through the fold), so per-line usage sums to the session totals; one with zero usage gets none. Abandoned branches are excluded. Read per-call usage from the full converted transcript. Pi user `image` items pass through verbatim in Pi's native shape (`data`, `mimeType`) and in source order, so an image-only user message still has a line; `data` is the inline base64, or an `entire-asset:assets/…` placeholder when image externalization (`redaction.externalize_images`) moved the image to the checkpoint's assets.

### Blocks

- User text: `{"id"?: string, "text": string}`. There is no `type` field (a v1 quirk).
- Assistant text: `{"type": "text", "text": string}`.
- Tool use: `{"type": "tool_use", "id"?: string, "name": string, "input": any, "result"?: {"output": string, "status": "success"|"error", "exitCode"?: int, "declined"?: bool, "cwd"?: string, "file"?: {"filePath": string, "numLines"?: int}, "matchCount"?: int, "agent"?: {"id": string}}}`.
  Tool results are inlined into the `tool_use` block that requested them,
  matched by tool call ID where the agent records one, including the results
  of parallel calls that the agent writes separately.
  `agent.id` is the agent's own ID for the subagent session or thread the call
  launched (never the tool call ID, which is the block's `id`), when the parent
  transcript records one: Claude Code's `toolUseResult.agentId` (Agent, and
  forked Skill calls), Codex's `SubAgentActivity` thread for a `spawn_agent`
  call, OpenCode's `task` session (`state.metadata.sessionId`), and Copilot's
  `subagent.started` agent for a task call.
  `exitCode` is the exit code of the command the call ran, when the agent
  records one: `0` is a recorded success, and absence means unknown, never
  success. `declined` is `true` for a call the user declined, which never
  ran; its `status` is `error`, as it was before the field existed, so a
  reader that only checks `status` counts it as failed. `cwd` is the
  working directory of the call as the agent records it. Only the Codex
  item path writes these three: a command's exit code and own `cwd`, and
  for a file change (whose paths are absolute) the `cwd` of its turn, from
  the rollout's latest `turn_context`. Older lines and other agents' lines
  have none of them.
- Image: passed through from the source verbatim. The image source is either
  inline base64 or an `entire-asset:assets/…` placeholder left by image
  externalization.
- Any other block type is passed through verbatim. Thinking blocks are dropped
  by the converters.

Codex: rollouts from Codex versions that record items (the first turn has a
user message `item_completed` event) convert item by item: each
`item_completed` item becomes its own line or lines.
Commands are `Bash` tool uses whose input is the script inside `<shell> -lc`
or `<shell> -c` (other commands are shown whole), with the command's output,
exit code and working directory; file changes are `FileChange` with each
file's diff, and their turn's working directory on the result; a command or
file change the user declined has an `error` result marked `declined`; MCP calls are named
`server.tool`; web searches are `WebSearch` and image views
`ImageView`; a sub-agent spawn is `spawn_agent`, an interrupt
`interrupt_agent` and any other interaction (a message or a follow-up task,
which the item doesn't tell apart) `interact_agent`, each with the
sub-agent's `agent.id`. Code-mode
wrapper calls no longer appear. Lines carry their item's time (RFC 3339 UTC
with milliseconds), and usage is per model call (see Per-call usage).
Items it can't read (such as one without an ID) or doesn't map (reasoning,
plans such as `update_plan`, compaction and other items) are skipped and
add no line. Older rollouts keep the `response_item` path, and so do
rollouts whose first turn has its prompt only as a `response_item` (a
guardian sub-session, whose agent message is an item) and thread_spawn
sub-agent rollouts (no items in the first turn, the task prompt as a
`response_item`).
A rollout takes the item path when its first turn (to its `task_complete`
or `turn_aborted`, or the next `task_started`) has a user message item.
`NewCodexRolloutAdapter` streams an item-path rollout with the same
mapping, and `CodexItemRolloutDecider`, fed the rollout as it grows, tells a
live reader when it can: a rollout still undecided once final takes the
`response_item` path.
`CodexNotificationRecords` maps a Codex app-server `item/started` or
`item/completed` notification to records with the same mapping, so a live
stream of a Codex session shows a completed item exactly as it is stored.
Its `CodexLive` argument carries what the stream knows beyond the item: the
agent text and command output so far, whether the turn ended while the item
was running (shown failed), a fallback time, and the turn's working
directory (`TurnCWD`, shown on a file change's result as the stored line
shows its `turn_context` cwd). Usage is not part of it:
a stream attaches each call's usage itself, as an `OpUsage` record.

### Evolution rules

1. Readers ignore unknown fields, keep unknown block types (available through
   `Block.Raw`), and return lines with an unknown `type` as they are, so
   consumers can skip them.
2. New fields, block types and line types are additive and optional. `v` stays `1`. Old v1 lines without the new usage and model fields remain valid.
3. `v` is bumped only for a breaking change.

## Reading

`Decode` returns every line it could read. If it skipped any, it also returns a
`*SkippedLinesError` listing each skipped line's 1-based physical line number
and the reason. Blank lines are ignored (but still counted in line numbers).

A line is skipped when it:

- is not a JSON object (including malformed JSON),
- has no `v`, or a `v` other than `1`,
- has no `type`, or
- has a known field of the wrong JSON type, for example `"agent": 42`
  or `"input_tokens": "x"` (reason `invalid field: <name>`). A `ts` that is
  not a string is ignored rather than skipped.

For optional scalar fields, JSON `null` is treated like absence, not a wrong
type: strings (including `model`) become empty, token totals (including the
historical `input_tokens` and `output_tokens`) become zero, and cache-write
splits remain unknown (`nil`). These values do not cause a line to be skipped.

`Decode` normalizes three v1 quirks:

- A block that has `text` but no `type` gets `Type` `"text"`, on any line type.
- A `content` value that is a JSON string becomes a single text block.
- A `content` value that is `null`, absent, or any other non-array, non-string
  JSON value becomes no blocks. The line is still returned.

Every block carries `Raw`, the block exactly as stored (for string content,
the synthesized text block). A block that is not a JSON object, or whose known
fields have the wrong JSON type, is returned with only `Raw` set; it never
causes its line to be skipped.

```go
lines, err := transcript.Decode(b)
// strict:   if err != nil { return err }
// tolerant: log err and use lines

var skipped *transcript.SkippedLinesError
if errors.As(err, &skipped) {
	for _, s := range skipped.Skipped {
		log.Printf("line %d: %s", s.Line, s.Reason)
	}
}
```

`Parse` accepts any supported format. Input whose first non-blank line is a JSON
object with an integer `v` and a non-empty string `type` is decoded as is and
the options are ignored. Anything else is converted first.

```go
lines, err := transcript.Parse(native, transcript.Options{Agent: "claude-code", CLIVersion: "0.5.1"})
```

To get one checkpoint's portion of a session, convert with the boundary and
slice the decoded lines:

```go
full, boundary, err := transcript.ConvertWithBoundary(native, transcript.Options{
	Agent: "claude-code", CLIVersion: "0.5.1", StartLine: checkpointStart,
})
if err != nil {
	return err
}
lines, err := transcript.Decode(full)
// ...
checkpointLines := lines[boundary:]
```

There is no general-purpose writer for the format; the converters and the fold
produce it.

## Records and fold

A `Record` is one append-only change to a transcript. Records are never revised
once emitted, so they can be streamed and stored as plain appends. `Fold`
applies records in order and returns the transcript lines.

In this repository the fold is used by `Convert`: for Claude Code, Cursor and
Droid, it runs a `JSONLAdapter` that turns the native transcript into records
and then folds them, for Pi a `PiAdapter`, and for OpenCode the records
`OpenCodeAdapter` sends for each message. The other converters still write
lines directly. The fold
is meant to be shared with a backend that folds the same records to show a live
session, so that a live view and a checkpoint's `transcript.jsonl` match byte
for byte.

A live producer uses the same adapter (`NewClaudeAdapter`, `NewCursorAdapter`,
`NewDroidAdapter`, `NewPiAdapter`; OpenCode's differs, see below). `Feed` accepts the transcript in chunks split anywhere and
returns the records for the lines it completed; `Flush` consumes a trailing
partial line and is called only once the transcript is final. Fold keys are
stable only when the adapter is fed from the transcript's first line, so a
producer that restarts replays from line 1. `Lines` reports how many source
lines have been consumed. Records carry the transcript's bytes as fed: redact
before feeding.

The Pi adapter keys each message by its Pi entry ID and sends it whole as a
`message` record, with its tool results spliced in; it sends the message again
when a result it shows changes, and `drop`s it when it leaves the active
branch (a `message` record restores it in place if the branch comes back). A
line that only grows the active branch is read without walking the tree, so a
session that only grows reads in linear time. Like the JSONL adapters, it has
no line size limit: a long line is held until its newline arrives and read
whole. `Convert` still fails on a Pi line of 10 MiB or more (newline
excluded), as it always has, so the fold matches `Convert` wherever `Convert`
succeeds.

### OpenCode

OpenCode keeps a session in its database and rewrites a message's rows in
place as the message grows, so there is no append-only transcript to feed.
A live producer exports the session again once it changes (`opencode export
<id>` on 1.x, `opencode session export --standalone <id>` on 2.x) and feeds
`OpenCodeAdapter` (`NewOpenCodeAdapter`) snapshot lines: one message per
line, `{"info":{...},"parts":[...]}` in the OpenCode 1 shape, as
`OpenCodeSnapshotLines` splits an export of either version
(a 2.x export is converted by the internal `opencodev2` package). `FeedExport` does both:
it feeds every message of an export in order, then drops the messages sent
before that the export no longer has (a revert or a compaction), in the
order they were first sent. A producer feeding lines itself calls
`Drop(messageID)` for those.

A pending revert (OpenCode's undo sets the session's `info.revert`; the
next prompt deletes the reverted messages, redo clears it) hides what
OpenCode hides: `OpenCodeSnapshotLines` leaves out the reverted message and
every later one, or, for a revert of one of its parts, that message's parts
from it on. So an undo drops them from the stream at once and a redo
restores them. `Convert` still writes them, as the database holds them
until the next prompt.

Each message is keyed by its `info.id` (also the assistant line's `id`) and
sent whole as a `message` record. It is sent again only when its record
changed: a repeated snapshot, or a change that does not show (a
`step-finish` part, a completion time), sends nothing, and a changed one
replaces the message under the same key. A dropped message's next snapshot
restores it where it was first created. Its tokens are a usage snapshot
(`input_tokens` and `output_tokens`, as `Convert` writes them), replaced
whole with the message. An assistant message with no text or tool parts is
sent with content `[]`, which the fold hides but which keeps its place; once
it has tokens it is sent with no content, a `"content":null` line carrying
its usage. A tool still `pending` or `running` has no `result` yet.

Folding every record from a sequence of snapshots equals `Convert` of the
export made of each message's latest snapshot, dropped messages left out,
when messages are first fed in session order (a message keeps the position at
which it was first fed) and message IDs are present and unique, as OpenCode
writes them. Lines that are not such a message, or whose role is neither
`user` nor `assistant`, are consumed and ignored; `Lines` counts them.

### Record wire format v1

One JSON object per record. An omitted field and a zero-length one mean the same: in Go, a nil or empty `json.RawMessage` is absent. This is about the field, not its JSON value: `content` of `[]` or `null` is present, and the visibility rules below treat it differently from absent content.

| Field | Type | Ops | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `op` | string | all | `message`, `append`, `result`, `usage` or `drop`. |
| `id` | string | all | The fold key: unique and stable within a session. Required. |
| `sourceId` | string | `message` | The agent's own message ID, printed as the line's `id`. Differs from `id` when the agent reuses an ID for a later, separate message. |
| `role` | string | `message` | `user` or `assistant`; becomes the line's `type`. Required on `message`. |
| `ts` | any JSON | `message`, `append` | Copied to the line's `ts` verbatim. An `append` without `ts` clears the timestamp. |
| `content` | any JSON | `message`, `append` | Normally an array of blocks. `message` replaces the content; `append` adds the blocks of an array and ignores anything else. Appending to content that is not an array discards that content, since it has no blocks. |
| `toolUseId` | string | `result` | The `tool_use` block to target, searching from the end. Empty targets the last `tool_use` block. |
| `result` | object | `result` | The tool result object described under Blocks. Required on `result`. |
| `usage` | object | `message`, `append`, `usage` | Optional per-call snapshot (`model`, `inputTokens`, `outputTokens`, `cacheReadTokens`, `cacheWriteTokens`, `cacheWrite5mTokens`, `cacheWrite1hTokens`, `reasoningTokens`). When present it replaces the message's whole snapshot, and the line's usage fields come from it instead of `inputTokens`/`outputTokens`. |
| `inputTokens`, `outputTokens` | int | `message`, `append`, `usage` | A non-zero value replaces the previous one; agents report cumulative usage. |

What each op does to the message `id` names:

- `message` creates it, or restates it: role, source ID, timestamp and content are replaced, token counts and any usage snapshot are updated, and a dropped message is restored. A message keeps the position where it was first created.
- `append` concatenates content blocks and replaces the timestamp. Appending to non-array content (a string, `null`, or none) replaces it with the appended blocks, possibly none: the result is always an array.
- `result` sets the result of one `tool_use` block. Nothing changes when the content is not an array, when one of its blocks is not an object, or when no block matches.
- `usage` updates token counts and, when it carries `usage`, the per-call snapshot.
- `drop` hides the message.

Every op except `message` must target a message created earlier, in this batch or a previous one.

Compatibility: new optional fields may be added, and readers ignore fields they do not know. A new op is a breaking change: `Apply` rejects a batch containing an op it does not know.

### Incremental folding

A `Folder` folds incrementally. `Apply` validates a whole batch before changing anything and returns the IDs of the messages it touched. `Line(id)` returns one message's current line, or not visible when the message is dropped or is an assistant message whose content is `[]` or `null`. An assistant message with no content at all is visible and prints `"content":null`, as `Convert` always has. A live view re-renders the touched messages and removes those that are no longer visible:

```go
f := transcript.NewFolder(transcript.Options{Agent: "claude-code", CLIVersion: "0.5.1"})
touched, err := f.Apply(records)
if err != nil {
	return err
}
for _, id := range touched {
	if line, ok := f.Line(id); ok {
		render(id, line)
	} else {
		remove(id)
	}
}
```

Decode each streamed record into a zero `Record`. `encoding/json` leaves fields the input omits unchanged, so a reused variable would carry an earlier `ts` into an `append` that has none.

### Resource use

A `Folder` keeps every message in memory and has no limits of its own. Applying a record costs time in the record's size, with one exception: the first `append` or `result` after a `message` record splits that record's content into blocks, once. Until an `append` or a matching `result` takes the split blocks over as the content, they are kept beside the original bytes, so such a message briefly costs twice its size. Producing a line costs time in that message's size, and `Lines` in the size of all messages. A caller folding records from an untrusted source must bound the number and size of records and messages itself.

content.text:
Yes for the transcript conversion (the `compact-transcript` command). The other transcript analysis can stay in Sarvam for now.

**The shared parser already exists.** It's the CLI's public package `github.com/entireio/cli/transcript`, and its converter recognises Codex rollouts from their content (`isCodexFormat` in `transcript/compact.go:106`). Sarvam's rollout is the Codex format: `session_meta`, `turn_context`, `response_item`, and `event_msg` with `token_count`. Sarvam doesn't need its own 247-line `compact.go`.

**I ran both converters on the same Sarvam rollout.** The rollout comes from the merged tests' fixture, plus a `turn_context`, two `token_count` events and a failed `exec_command`.

| | Sarvam `compact.go` (merged) | Shared `transcript.Convert` |
|---|---|---|
| Model and per-call token usage | **None** | Yes: model, fresh input, `cache_read_tokens` and output for each call, computed correctly |
| Line grouping | One line per item | One line per model call, matching how Codex is stored |
| Exec result `{"output":"","metadata":{"exit_code":1}}` | Correct: `status: error` | **Wrong**: `status: success`, and the raw JSON wrapper shown as the output |
| Newer Codex item-based rollouts, checkpoint slicing | No | Yes |

So Sarvam's checkpoints currently carry no per-call usage or model. The shared converter has one gap: on this rollout path it doesn't decode the `metadata.exit_code` wrapper. That's the bug the trail's last finding fixed in Sarvam's copy.

**Recommended path:**
1. In the CLI repo, teach `transcript/codex.go` to decode the `{"output", "metadata":{"exit_code"}}` wrapper on `function_call_output` and set `status` and `exitCode` from it. This is Codex's shell output shape, so it isn't Sarvam-specific.
2. In Sarvam, stop advertising `compact_transcript` and delete `compact.go` and its tests. When an agent has no compactor, the CLI falls back to its built-in one (`checkpoint/persistent.go:1156-1163`), which detects the Codex format. That adds no dependency and needs no Go version bump. I'd avoid importing the package into the agent instead: the CLI module declares `go 1.27.4` and Sarvam is on `1.26.0`, so it would force a bump and tie the agent to CLI releases.
3. The other analysis code (token counting in `tokens.go`, changed-file and prompt extraction) stays as it is. The shared package doesn't provide those functions. Token counting could later sum the usage from `transcript.Parse`, but that's optional.

**The other external agents don't need this.** Hermes, kiro, goose, amp, qwen and the rest each read a format of their own, so their hand-written compactors are justified. Sarvam is the only one whose format the CLI already handles.

content.text:
Yes, but through the protocol rather than by having agents import the package.

**External agents can already use it in two ways, and neither is good:**

1. **Import `github.com/entireio/cli/transcript`.** It's a public package that only uses the standard library, and the CLI has a test that keeps it that way. But the CLI module declares `go 1.27.4`, so every agent that imports it has to move to that Go version (Sarvam is on 1.26). The agent also has to pin a CLI version, and fixes made in the CLI only reach the agent when someone bumps that pin.
2. **Leave out `compact_transcript`, so the CLI uses its built-in converter.** For Sarvam this would have worked, because the converter recognises the Codex format from the file content. Nothing says so, though. The protocol spec (`external-agent-protocol.md:355`) only mentions the built-in converter as what runs when an agent's own converter fails. This repo's skill files (`.claude/skills/entire-external-agent/`) don't mention transcript conversion at all. The Sarvam authors had no way to know they could skip writing `compact.go`.

**What I'd do:**

- **Have agents declare their native format explicitly.** For example, an optional `transcript_format: "codex"` in the agent's `info` response (the field name is only a suggestion). The CLI would then run its own converter for that format, labelled with the agent's name. This is better than relying on content detection, which is undocumented and could guess wrong. Sarvam would declare `codex` and delete `compact.go`. Format fixes would reach every agent with each CLI release, at no cost to the agent.
- **Update the research step in the skill.** When the target agent's transcript is a format the CLI already converts (Claude-style JSONL, Codex, Pi, OpenCode, Gemini, Copilot, Droid), the agent should declare that format and not write a converter. Only formats the CLI doesn't know should get their own `compact-transcript`, as hermes, kiro and goose correctly do today.
- **Fix the CLI converter's gap first.** On older Codex rollouts it doesn't read the `{"output", "metadata":{"exit_code"}}` wrapper around command results, so a failed command shows as a success. Sarvam's own converter handles this; the shared one doesn't yet.
- **Keep importing the package as an option for agents with a custom format that is close to a known one.** It shouldn't be the default.

The trade-off: an agent that relies on the CLI's converter can't patch quirks in its own format, and has to wait for a CLI release. For forks of agents the CLI already supports, like Sarvam, that's the right trade: one well-tested converter instead of a partial copy, which here was missing the model and per-call token usage.

# Entire CLI — repository instructions

Go CLI built with Cobra and Charmbracelet Huh. `AGENTS.md` is a symlink to this
file. Keep this entry point short: repo-wide rules and pointers, not command
catalogs, implementation histories, or subsystem specifications.

## Project map

- `cmd/entire/`: entry point and external-command dispatch.
- `cmd/entire/cli/`: Cobra commands, group roots, and CLI helpers. Group/verb files
  use `<noun>_group.go` and `<noun>_<verb>.go`.
- `cmd/entire/cli/agent/`: built-in agent integrations and external-agent protocol.
- `cmd/entire/cli/strategy/`: manual-commit strategy and lifecycle/git hooks.
- `cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/`: persistent checkpoint storage (written at commit).
- `cmd/entire/cli/session/`: session state shared across worktrees.
- `cmd/entire/cli/integration_test/`: simulated-hook integration tests.
- `e2e/`: real-agent tests and deterministic Vogon canary.
- `internal/entireclient/`: API clients, authentication, and user directories.

Use the Go version pinned by `go.mod` and tools configured in `mise.toml`.
For installed CLI usage, run `entire agent-help`, then
`entire agent-help <command>` for current flags; do not guess from a static list.

## Read when relevant

Read the applicable reference **before changing that area**, not every reference
at session start. Follow its related links when the task crosses those boundaries.

| Area being changed | Reference |
| --- | --- |
| Commands, help, experimental visibility, repo refs, prompts | [CLI conventions](docs/development/cli-conventions.md) |
| Test harnesses, isolation, TTY behavior, source guards | [Testing](docs/development/testing.md) |
| Filesystem I/O, `.entire`, symlinks, hook configs, root anchors | [Filesystem safety](docs/development/filesystem-safety.md) |
| Git operations, executable lookup, subprocesses, Windows launching | [Git and subprocess safety](docs/development/git-safety.md) |
| Caller identification or session current/tokens/adopt | [Caller-session resolution](docs/development/caller-session-resolution.md) |
| Control-plane auth or data-plane routing | [API routing](docs/development/api-routing.md) |

## Verification

| Task | Command / requirement |
| --- | --- |
| Unit tests | `mise run test` |
| Integration tests | `mise run test:integration`; required when changing integration test code |
| Deterministic E2E canary | `mise run test:e2e:canary`; safe without API calls |
| All CI tests | `mise run test:ci` (unit + integration + canary) |
| Format and lint | `mise run fmt && mise run lint` |
| Before every commit | **`mise run check`** (format, lint, all CI tests) |
| Before any push or remote code update | **`mise run lint` on the current tree**, after the latest formatting pass |
| After every push to an open PR | **check the trail's findings** (`entire trail finding list cli/<n> --freshness any`; `<n>` is the PR branch's cli trail number, not the PR number); fix real ones, resolve with `-m`, and re-check after the fix lands. Not done until findings are clear |
| Duplication checks | `mise run dup` or `mise run dup:staged`; normal lint also checks duplication |
| Complexity gate | `mise run complexity:gate`; CI fails a PR on functions over cognitive complexity 30 that are new or worsened against the merge base. The threshold is a gate flag (`COGNIT_WARN`), not a `.golangci.yaml` setting |
| Windows installer | `mise run test:ps1`; see testing reference for prerequisites |

**Do not run real-agent E2E tests unless the user explicitly requests them.** They
make paid API calls. Vogon is the exception: its canary is deterministic and free.
When changing E2E prompt wording, run the canary and update Vogon's regex parsing
if needed. Formatting can rewrite files; an earlier lint pass is not sufficient.

Before implementing Go code, search nearby packages and helpers for reusable
patterns. Use `/go:discover-related` when available, otherwise `rg` and related
implementations/tests. Check `.golangci.yaml`; handle errors and avoid duplication.

## Test safety

- Every top-level test and subtest calls `t.Parallel()` unless it changes
  process-global state (`t.Chdir`, `t.Setenv`, or their `os` equivalents).
- Git tests use isolated temporary repositories, preferably
  `testutil.InitRepo(t, dir)` plus its file/add/commit helpers. Redirect CWD before
  calling CWD-based handlers. Never mutate the real checkout's git/session state.
- Tests must not access the developer's real config, cache, or keychain.
  In-process fallbacks are shared per process; use per-test overrides and
  `tokenstore.UseFileBackendForTesting` when isolation between tests is needed.
  Tests that can reach the OS keyring need `keyring.MockInit()` in `TestMain`.
- Spawned binaries do not inherit Go's test detection. Harnesses must isolate
  `ENTIRE_CONFIG_DIR`, `XDG_CACHE_HOME`, `ENTIRE_TOKEN_STORE=file`,
  `ENTIRE_TOKEN_STORE_PATH`, and `ENTIRE_TEST_AUTH_STORE_FILE`.
- Prefer `execx.NonInteractive` for real CLI/git test subprocesses so a developer's
  terminal cannot make them prompt or hang.
- Caller-resolution tests clear every variable from `agent.CallerSessionEnvVars()`;
  never hand-maintain a partial list or inherit the developer's agent identity.
- Source-scanning guards discover files through testutil's guard helpers
  (`GitGrepGuard`, `GuardGoFiles`), restrict pathspecs to Go files, and fail on
  zero matches. Do not weaken guard ledgers to silence failures.

## Filesystem and settings safety

**Use the existing anchor for each tree; never assemble a path and perform bare
I/O beneath it.** Read the filesystem reference before adding or changing I/O.

| Tree | Canonical owner |
| --- | --- |
| `.entire` | `entiredir` |
| Git common directory | `gitdir` |
| Working tree | `worktreedir` |
| Agent hook configuration | `agent.HookConfigFile` |
| Agent session store | `agent.SessionStore` |
| Active git hooks directory | `strategy.hooksRootForInstall` / `ForRemoval` |
| Per-user config/cache | `userdirs.ConfigRoot` / `CacheRoot` |
| Managed plugins | `pluginRoot` |

- Root bases come from trusted resolvers, **not `filepath.Dir(target)`**. Confining
  a file to its own derived parent proves nothing. Prefer an existing anchor.
- Roots share the `osroot.Shared` registry. Open child roots with
  `osroot.SharedChild` / `OpenChild`, not bare `parent.OpenRoot`.
- Use `osroot` operations and `jsonutil.WriteFileAtomicIn` / `CreateTempIn`.
  Directories use `MkdirAllNoSymlink`; rooted read-only operations must also
  enforce symlink policy. Atomic writes replace leaf links rather than follow them.
- `.entire` must be a real directory; validate through
  `paths.ValidateEntireDirAt` / `RequireEntireDir`. Do not treat an unresolved
  repository as absent. Settings reads must also refuse symlinks themselves.
- Do not broaden symlink exceptions. Developer-vouched agent config directories

content.text:
The draft is ready in a new CLI worktree. It isn't committed or pushed yet.

- **Location:** `/Users/peytonmontei/dev/entire/devenv/entireio/cli-transcript-format`
- **Branch:** `peyton/external-transcript-format`, based on `origin/main`

## What it does

**Protocol.** An external agent can add `"transcript_format": "codex"` (or another format the CLI already converts) to its `info` response, and leave `compact_transcript` off. The CLI's own converter then builds that agent's `transcript.jsonl`, labelled with the agent's name. If the CLI doesn't recognise the value (for example, an agent built for a newer CLI), it ignores it and falls back to detecting the format from the transcript.

**Shared converter (`github.com/entireio/cli/transcript`):**
- `transcript/format.go` adds format names matching the built-in agents (`claude-code`, `cursor`, `codex`, `copilot-cli`, `factoryai-droid`, `gemini`, `opencode`, `pi`) and a `KnownFormat` check.
- `Options.Format` picks the converter directly. When it's empty, the format is detected as before. `Convert` was rewritten to go through the new `detectFormat`/`convertAs` functions.
- A declared `claude-code` format uses Claude Code's per-call token counting even when the agent has a different name. Before, only an agent literally named `claude-code` got it.
- `transcript/codex.go` now reads the older Codex shell result `{"output", "metadata":{"exit_code"}}`. A non-zero exit code marks the call as failed, and the inner output is unwrapped. Current Codex writes plain text instead, which is left as it is.

**CLI wiring.**
- `InfoResponse.TranscriptFormat` stores the declared value.
- A new `TranscriptFormatProvider` interface is reached through `agent.AsTranscriptFormatProvider`. A guard test requires that helper rather than a direct type check.
- `persistent.go` passes the declared format to the built-in converter when the agent has none of its own.

**Docs.** `external-agent-protocol.md` documents the `info` field and says to declare a format instead of writing a converter. `transcript/README.md` covers `Options.Format` and the new exit-code source.

## Verification

- **Tests added:**
  - A declared format gives byte-identical output to detection for every format's sample transcript, both from line 0 and from line 3.
  - Declaring `claude-code` gives Claude Code's token counting to another agent's name.
  - An unknown format returns an error.
  - Four cases for the exit-code wrapper.
  - `info` with a known, unknown, or missing format.
  - Two checkpoint tests. With the format declared, the stored `transcript.jsonl` includes the model. Without it, the model is missing.
- **Checks run:** the affected packages pass (`transcript`, `agent/...`, `checkpoint`, `summarize`, `cli/transcript`), along with `mise run lint` (0 issues) and `mise run complexity:gate`. I did not run the full `mise run check` or the integration tests.
- **End to end:** the earlier Sarvam rollout, converted with `Format: codex`, now gets the model and per-call tokens, and the failed `false` command shows `status: error, exitCode: 1`. Sarvam's own converter got the status right but had no usage; the shared converter had usage but marked the failure a success.

## Not in this draft

- **Summaries:** `summarize.BuildCondensedTranscriptFromBytes` still treats every external agent's transcript as Claude-style JSONL. Making summaries honour `transcript_format` would be a small follow-up.
- **Sarvam:** declaring `transcript_format: "codex"` and deleting its `compact.go` and the `compact_transcript` capability goes in this repo once a CLI release with this change ships.
- **Skill update:** the research step in `.claude/skills/entire-external-agent/` should say to check for a known format first.

## Subcommands

### Always Required

#### `info`

Returns agent metadata and declared capabilities.

**Arguments:** None

**Output (stdout):** JSON

```json
{
  "protocol_version": 1,
  "name": "cursor",
  "type": "Cursor",
  "description": "Cursor - AI-powered code editor",
  "protected_dirs": [".cursor"],
  "hook_names": ["session-start", "session-end", "stop"],
  "capabilities": {
    "hooks": true,
    "transcript_analyzer": true,
    "transcript_preparer": false,
    "token_calculator": false,
    "text_generator": false,
    "hook_response_writer": false,
    "subagent_aware_extractor": false
  }
}
```

The `capabilities` object determines which optional subcommands the CLI will call. If a capability is `false` or missing, the CLI will never invoke the corresponding subcommands.

Optional: `"caller_env_vars": ["MYAGENT_SESSION_ID"]` lists environment variables the agent sets for the commands it runs (uppercase names only). `entire review` uses them to recognise the agent as the caller, so it refuses to approve reviews of someone else's code on the user's behalf and names the agent when one passes `--trust-target`. Agents that set the cross-tool `AI_AGENT` variable are recognised without declaring it.

Optional: `"transcript_format": "codex"` declares that the agent's native transcript is written in a format the CLI already converts, so the CLI's built-in compactor builds its `transcript.jsonl` (see [`compact_transcript`](#capability-compact_transcript)). Use it when the agent is a fork of, or writes the same transcript as, a built-in agent. Values: `claude-code`, `cursor`, `codex`, `copilot-cli`, `factoryai-droid`, `gemini`, `opencode`, `pi`. A value this CLI does not know is ignored, and the format is detected from the transcript.

#### `detect`

Checks whether the agent is present/usable in the current environment.

**Arguments:** None

**Output (stdout):** JSON

```json
{"present": true}
```

#### `get-session-id`

Extracts the session ID from a hook input event.

**Input (stdin):** JSON — the [HookInput object](#hookinput-object)

**Output (stdout):** JSON

```json
{"session_id": "abc123"}
```

#### `get-session-dir --repo-path <path>`

Returns the directory where agent sessions are stored.

**Arguments:**
- `--repo-path` — Absolute path to the repository

**Output (stdout):** JSON

```json
{"session_dir": "/path/to/sessions"}
```

#### `resolve-session-file --session-dir <dir> --session-id <id>`

Resolves the session file path from a session directory and ID.

**Arguments:**
- `--session-dir` — Session directory path
- `--session-id` — Session identifier

**Output (stdout):** JSON

```json
{"session_file": "/path/to/session/file.jsonl"}
```

#### `read-session`

Reads session data from a hook input event.

**Input (stdin):** JSON — the [HookInput object](#hookinput-object)

**Output (stdout):** JSON — [AgentSession object](#agentsession-object)

```json
{
  "session_id": "abc123",
  "agent_name": "cursor",
  "repo_path": "/path/to/repo",
  "session_ref": "/path/to/file.jsonl",
  "start_time": "2026-01-13T12:00:00Z",
  "native_data": null,
  "modified_files": ["src/main.go"],
  "new_files": [],
  "deleted_files": []
}
```

#### `write-session`

Writes/updates session data.

**Input (stdin):** JSON — the [AgentSession object](#agentsession-object)

**Output:** Exit 0 on success.

#### `read-transcript --session-ref <path>`

Reads a transcript file and returns its raw bytes.

**Arguments:**
- `--session-ref` — Path to the transcript file

**Output (stdout):** Raw transcript bytes.

#### `chunk-transcript --max-size <n>`

Splits a transcript into chunks for storage.

**Input (stdin):** Raw transcript bytes.

**Arguments:**
- `--max-size` — Maximum chunk size in bytes

**Output (stdout):** JSON

```json
{"chunks": ["<base64-encoded-chunk>", "..."]}
```

#### `reassemble-transcript`

Reassembles transcript chunks back into a full transcript.

**Input (stdin):** JSON

```json
{"chunks": ["<base64-encoded-chunk>", "..."]}
```

**Output (stdout):** Raw transcript bytes.

#### `format-resume-command --session-id <id>`

Returns the command a user can run to resume a session.

**Arguments:**
- `--session-id` — Session identifier

**Output (stdout):** JSON

```json
{"command": "cursor --resume abc123"}
```

### Capability: `hooks`

These subcommands are required when `capabilities.hooks` is `true`.

# no compact_transcript), driven by simulated hook payloads. No model calls.
set -eu
E2E=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)
RUN="$E2E/run"
rm -rf "$RUN"
mkdir -p "$RUN/home" "$RUN/sarvam/sessions/2026/11/24" "$RUN/repo"

GIT_DIR_BIN=$(dirname "$(command -v git)")
export HOME="$RUN/home"
export PATH="$E2E/bin:$GIT_DIR_BIN:/usr/bin:/bin"
export ENTIRE_CONFIG_DIR="$RUN/home/.config/entire"
export XDG_CONFIG_HOME="$RUN/home/.config"
export XDG_CACHE_HOME="$RUN/home/.cache"
export ENTIRE_TOKEN_STORE=file
export ENTIRE_TOKEN_STORE_PATH="$RUN/home/tokens.json"
export ENTIRE_TEST_AUTH_STORE_FILE="$RUN/home/auth.json"
export ENTIRE_TELEMETRY_OPTOUT=1
export SARVAM_HOME="$RUN/sarvam"
export GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL="$RUN/home/.gitconfig"

git config --global user.email "e2e@example.invalid"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main

SID=01a1e2d3-8a2b-7dc2-b125-885a43ce43f5
ROLLOUT="$SARVAM_HOME/sessions/2026/11/24/rollout-2026-11-24T06-00-00-$SID.jsonl"
REPO="$RUN/repo"

cd "$REPO"
git init -q
echo "# test" > README.md
git add README.md && git commit -qm "initial"
entire enable --agent sarvam --telemetry=false >"$RUN/enable.log" 2>&1 || { cat "$RUN/enable.log"; exit 1; }
git add -A && git commit -qm "enable entire" || true

hook() { # name payload-json

}
payload() { # event extra-json

{"timestamp":"2026-11-24T06:00:00.000Z","type":"session_meta","payload":{"id":"$SID","cwd":"$REPO","source":"cli","cli_version":"0.58.0"}}
{"timestamp":"2026-11-24T06:00:00.100Z","type":"turn_context","payload":{"cwd":"$REPO","model":"sarvam-m"}}

hook session-start "$(payload SessionStart ',"source":"startup"')"

PROMPT='Create hi.txt with hi, then run false'

{"timestamp":"2026-11-24T06:00:01.000Z","type":"response_item","payload":{"type":"message","role":"user","content":[{"type":"input_text","text":"$PROMPT"}]}}

{"timestamp":"2026-11-24T06:00:03.000Z","type":"response_item","payload":{"type":"function_call","name":"exec_command","call_id":"call-2","arguments":"{\"cmd\":\"false\"}"}}
{"timestamp":"2026-11-24T06:00:03.100Z","type":"response_item","payload":{"type":"function_call_output","call_id":"call-2","output":"{\"output\":\"\",\"metadata\":{\"exit_code\":1}}"}}
{"timestamp":"2026-11-24T06:00:03.200Z","type":"response_item","payload":{"type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"output_text","text":"done"}]}}
{"timestamp":"2026-11-24T06:00:03.300Z","type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"token_count","info":{"total_token_usage":{"input_tokens":150,"cached_input_tokens":50,"output_tokens":25,"total_tokens":175},"last_token_usage":{"input_tokens":50,"cached_input_tokens":10,"output_tokens":5,"total_tokens":55}}}}

hook stop "$(payload Stop ',"stop_hook_active":false,"last_assistant_message":"done"')"

git add hi.txt && git commit -qm "add hi.txt" >"$RUN/commit.log" 2>&1 || { cat "$RUN/commit.log"; exit 1; }

echo "== commit trailers"

echo "== checkpoint refs"

for ref in $(git for-each-ref --format='%(refname)' | grep -v 'refs/heads'); do

    echo "-- $ref:$p"; git show "$ref:$p"

done

The local end-to-end run passes. With the draft CLI, a real external agent that declares `transcript_format: codex` and has no converter of its own gets a correct `transcript.jsonl` through the normal checkpoint flow. Nothing was pushed and no model was called.

**How I ran it:** I built `entire` from the draft branch, plus a local copy of the real Sarvam binary changed to declare `transcript_format: codex` and turn off its own converter. I ran them in a throwaway repo with its own HOME, config and Sarvam session folder. The script runs `entire enable --agent sarvam`, then sends session-start, prompt and stop hook payloads while a Codex-style transcript grows (two commands, one of them a failing `false`, and two token-count events), then commits. Each run produced a checkpoint, and I read its `transcript.jsonl`.

| Run | Model and per-call tokens | Line grouping | Failed `false` command |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Draft CLI + Sarvam declaring `codex`** | Yes (`sarvam-m`, input 60/40, cache read 40/10, output 20/5) | One line per model call | `status: error`, `exitCode: 1`, output unwrapped |
| Released CLI + Sarvam as merged (today) | None | One line per item | `status: error`, from Sarvam's own converter |
| Released CLI + Sarvam declaring `codex` | Yes | One line per model call | **Wrong:** `success`, with the raw wrapper text as output |

- **The first row is the change working.** Sarvam's own converter was switched off in that run, so the model and token fields can only have come from the CLI's converter, and the exit code shows the new wrapper decoding.
- **The third row confirms the change is safe for older CLIs.** A released CLI ignores the unknown `info` field, falls back to recognising the transcript as Codex, and still writes a checkpoint. Only the exit-code fix needs the new CLI.

Two things to know:
- In the third row, the released CLI's converter ran even without the new field, because Sarvam's converter was off and the CLI recognised the format on its own. For Codex, what the declared format adds is an explicit, documented choice instead of a guess. It changes the result for JSONL agents not named `claude-code`, which only get per-call usage when they declare that format; the checkpoint unit test covers that case.

Plugins are TypeScript/JavaScript modules loaded at startup from `.kilo/plugins/` and run on Bun. The integration installs a project plugin that subscribes to the bus and forwards five lifecycle hooks (`session-start`, `turn-start`, `turn-end`, `compaction`, `session-end`) to the Entire CLI. The plugin uses Kilo's native event bus directly — `session.idle` is deprecated upstream and `session.status` with `status.type === "idle"` is the reliable turn-end signal in both interactive and `kilo run` modes.

The plugin's `turn-end` fires **synchronously** and carries only `session_id` + `model`: `kilo run` exits on the same idle event, so an awaited in-plugin fetch could be cancelled before the hook runs. Turn-end payloads that do carry messages are still honored, but an empty message set never overwrites an existing transcript.

content.text:
The declared format helps two other merged agents, Oh My Pi (omp) and Kilo, not just Sarvam. For omp it's the only way the CLI's converter works at all, because it can't recognise omp's files on its own. I checked every agent in this repo and tested the two that write a format the CLI already knows, using their own test transcripts.

| Agent | Built on | CLI, format detected | CLI, format declared | That agent's own converter |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **omp (Oh My Pi)** | Pi | **Broken.** omp writes a title line before the Pi header, so detection misses Pi and treats the file as Claude-style lines. Tool calls stay raw and there's no usage. | Correct with `pi`, and it adds the **model**, which omp's own converter doesn't write | Correct, no model |
| **Kilo** | OpenCode | **Empty output.** Kilo stores one OpenCode message per line, not an OpenCode export. | Matches Kilo's own output with the new `opencode-messages` format. The only difference is an extra part ID on the user text. | Correct |
| Sarvam | Codex | Works | Works, and the exit-code fix applies | No model or usage |

Not candidates: amp, goose, grok, hermes and kiro use formats of their own, and qwen stores its own sidecar file. They should keep their own converters.

**Changes to the draft from this round:**
- **New `opencode-messages` format** for Kilo's layout (one OpenCode message per line). It reuses the CLI's existing OpenCode adapter, so there is no new parsing code. The CLI never guesses this format; an agent has to declare it.
- **Two new tests:**
  - The one-message-per-line form converts exactly like the export it came from, both from the start and from a later checkpoint.
  - A Pi session with a title line first: detection gets it wrong (the test checks that), and declaring `pi` gives the same output as a normal Pi session.
- **Docs:** the protocol doc lists the new value. The README explains the three cases where declaring a format behaves differently from detection: Claude Code token counting for other agent names, Pi with a leading title line, and the OpenCode one-message-per-line form.

**Behaviour differences omp or Kilo would see if they switched (not bugs, but worth knowing):**
- **omp tool names:** the CLI keeps omp's names as written (`Write`, `mcp:read`), while omp's own converter lowercases them and strips the `mcp:` prefix (`write`, `read`).
- **omp images:** user images are passed through instead of dropped.
- **Malformed blocks:** the CLI's Pi converter drops a whole message if one content block isn't an object. omp's own test includes such a block on purpose; real Pi sessions don't write them.

**Verification:** all affected CLI packages pass, along with lint (0 issues) and the complexity gate. The scratch test files I used to dump omp and Kilo transcripts are deleted, and `.worktrees/sarvam-review` is clean. The full end-to-end checkpoint run was only done with Sarvam. For omp and Kilo I compared conversions directly, since the checkpoint wiring is shared.

The CLI branch is still uncommitted in `../cli-transcript-format`. Do you want me to commit it and open the PR on `entireio/cli`?
so this fixes the two other agents?

No, not by itself. The two other agents aren't broken today, so there's nothing for this change to fix.

**Today:**
- omp and Kilo both declare `compact_transcript` and use their own converters. Those produce correct transcripts.
- The broken and empty results in my table only happen if they drop their converters and let the CLI guess the format. They don't do that today.

**What the change gives them:** the option to delete their own converters and use the CLI's shared one, if each agent makes a small follow-up:
- **omp:** declare `"transcript_format": "pi"` and turn off `compact_transcript`. It would also gain the model on each call, which its converter doesn't write. Without the declared format this switch isn't possible, because the CLI can't recognise omp's files.
- **Kilo:** declare `"transcript_format": "opencode-messages"` and turn off `compact_transcript`. The output stays essentially the same; the benefit is less code to maintain.

Each switch also needs a CLI release containing this change. On an older CLI that ignores the field, omp's transcript would come out broken and Kilo's empty, so they should keep their converters until the minimum supported CLI includes the change. They would also pick up the small differences I listed (omp's tool names and images).

The only behaviour this change improves without anyone acting is the exit-code fix. It applies to any Codex-format transcript the CLI converts itself, including built-in Codex sessions from older versions.

So it's an enabler, not a fix: it makes the shared converter usable by forks, and omp is the strongest case, since it gains model data it doesn't have today. Do you still want me to open the CLI PR on that basis?

input.command:
cd /Users/peytonmontei/dev/entire/devenv/entireio/cli-transcript-format && gh pr create --repo entireio/cli --base main --head peyton/external-transcript-format --title "Let external agents declare a built-in transcript format" --body-file - <<'EOF'
## Why

External agents that are forks of built-in agents each ship their own `compact-transcript`, re-implementing a converter the CLI already has. Those copies drift: Sarvam Code's (a Codex fork) writes no per-call model or usage, and Oh My Pi's (Pi) writes no model. Detection can't stand in for them either: Oh My Pi writes a title line before the Pi header, so it's not recognised as Pi, and Kilo Code stores one OpenCode message per line rather than an export, so it converts to nothing.

## What

- **Protocol:** an optional `"transcript_format"` field in `info`. An agent that declares it can leave `compact_transcript` off, and the CLI's built-in converter builds its `transcript.jsonl`, labelled with the agent's name. A value this CLI doesn't know is ignored, so the CLI falls back to detecting the format.
- **`transcript` library:**
  - `Options.Format` selects the converter instead of detecting it. The names match the built-in agents, plus `opencode-messages` (one `{"info","parts"}` message per line, never detected).
  - A declared `claude-code` gets per-call usage for any agent name.
  - A declared `pi` converts a session whose header isn't the first line.
- **Codex exit codes:** the `response_item` path now reads the `{"output","metadata":{"exit_code"}}` envelope that older Codex shell tools (and forks) write. A failed command becomes `status: error` with its `exitCode`, instead of `success` with the raw envelope as output.
- **Wiring:** `InfoResponse.TranscriptFormat`, reached through `agent.AsTranscriptFormatProvider`. The checkpoint fallback passes the declared format.
- **Docs:** the protocol spec (`info` field, plus guidance under `compact_transcript`) and `transcript/README.md`.

## Testing

- **Unit:**
  - A declared format gives byte-identical output to detection for every fixture, at `StartLine` 0 and 3.
  - `claude-code` for another agent name.
  - Unknown format.
  - `opencode-messages` matches the export it came from.
  - A Pi session with a leading title line: detection fails, the declared format succeeds.
  - Four exit-envelope cases.
  - `info` with a known, unknown, or missing format.
  - Checkpoint: a declared format changes the stored `transcript.jsonl` (the model is present), and without it the model is missing.
- **Against real agents' own fixtures:**
  - **Oh My Pi, declared `pi`:** matches its own converter and adds the model. It keeps native tool names (`Write`, `mcp:read`) where omp lowercases them and strips the `mcp:` prefix.
  - **Kilo, declared `opencode-messages`:** matches its own output.
- **Local end-to-end:**
  - A real `entire-agent-sarvam` binary, patched to declare `codex` with no compactor, ran through `entire enable`, simulated session-start, prompt and stop hooks, then a commit. The checkpoint's `transcript.jsonl` carries the model, per-call tokens and a failed command marked as an error.
  - The same agent against a released CLI still checkpoints, because the unknown field is ignored.
- **Suites:**
  - `mise run lint`: 0 issues.
  - `complexity:gate`: passes.
  - `go test -tags=integration -race ./...`: passes.
  - Integration suite: passes.
  - Canary: Vogon and roger-roger pass.
  - Under full-suite load, a few timing-sensitive tests in unrelated packages timed out (`claudecode`/`opencode` probes, fetch timeout). They pass when re-run individually.

## Follow-ups (not in this PR)

- Summaries (`summarize.BuildCondensedTranscriptFromBytes`) still treat external agents as Claude-style JSONL.
- Agents in `entireio/external-agents` can opt in once a release with this ships. Oh My Pi is the clearest win, since it gains the model.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF

## Why

External agents that are forks of built-in agents each ship their own `compact-transcript`, re-implementing a converter the CLI already has. Those copies drift: Sarvam Code's (a Codex fork) writes no per-call model or usage, and Oh My Pi's (Pi) writes no model. Detection can't stand in for them either: Oh My Pi writes a title line before the Pi header, so it's not recognised as Pi, and Kilo Code stores one OpenCode message per line rather than an export, so it converts to nothing.

## What

- **Protocol:** an optional `"transcript_format"` field in `info`. An agent that declares it can leave `compact_transcript` off, and the CLI's built-in converter builds its `transcript.jsonl`, labelled with the agent's name. A value this CLI doesn't know is ignored, so the CLI falls back to detecting the format.
- **`transcript` library:**
  - `Options.Format` selects the converter instead of detecting it. The names match the built-in agents, plus `opencode-messages` (one `{"info","parts"}` message per line, never detected).
  - A declared `claude-code` gets per-call usage for any agent name.
  - A declared `pi` converts a session whose header isn't the first line.
- **Codex exit codes:** the `response_item` path now reads the `{"output","metadata":{"exit_code"}}` envelope that older Codex shell tools (and forks) write. A failed command becomes `status: error` with its `exitCode`, instead of `success` with the raw envelope as output.
- **Wiring:** `InfoResponse.TranscriptFormat`, reached through `agent.AsTranscriptFormatProvider`. The checkpoint fallback passes the declared format.
- **Docs:** the protocol spec (`info` field, plus guidance under `compact_transcript`) and `transcript/README.md`.

## Testing

- **Unit:**
  - A declared format gives byte-identical output to detection for every fixture, at `StartLine` 0 and 3.
  - `claude-code` for another agent name.
  - Unknown format.
  - `opencode-messages` matches the export it came from.
  - A Pi session with a leading title line: detection fails, the declared format succeeds.
  - Four exit-envelope cases.
  - `info` with a known, unknown, or missing format.
  - Checkpoint: a declared format changes the stored `transcript.jsonl` (the model is present), and without it the model is missing.
- **Against real agents' own fixtures:**
  - **Oh My Pi, declared `pi`:** matches its own converter and adds the model. It keeps native tool names (`Write`, `mcp:read`) where omp lowercases them and strips the `mcp:` prefix.
  - **Kilo, declared `opencode-messages`:** matches its own output.
- **Local end-to-end:**
  - A real `entire-agent-sarvam` binary, patched to declare `codex` with no compactor, ran through `entire enable`, simulated session-start, prompt and stop hooks, then a commit. The checkpoint's `transcript.jsonl` carries the model, per-call tokens and a failed command marked as an error.
  - The same agent against a released CLI still checkpoints, because the unknown field is ignored.
- **Suites:**
  - `mise run lint`: 0 issues.
  - `complexity:gate`: passes.
  - `go test -tags=integration -race ./...`: passes.
  - Integration suite: passes.
  - Canary: Vogon and roger-roger pass.
  - Under full-suite load, a few timing-sensitive tests in unrelated packages timed out (`claudecode`/`opencode` probes, fetch timeout). They pass when re-run individually.

## Follow-ups (not in this PR)

- Summaries (`summarize.BuildCondensedTranscriptFromBytes`) still treat external agents as Claude-style JSONL.
- Agents in `entireio/external-agents` can opt in once a release with this ships. Oh My Pi is the clearest win, since it gains the model.

The external protocol gains optional **`transcript_format`** on `info`; the CLI reads it through **`TranscriptFormatProvider`** / `AsTranscriptFormatProvider` and passes it into checkpoint compaction via **`compactFields`** so `transcript.jsonl` is built with the right converter and labeled with the agent’s name.

I fixed the Codex finding and pushed it as commit a74761ed51. CI and the trail reviewers are still running on it.

**The fix:** the converter now reads the `{"output","metadata":{"exit_code"}}` envelope only when both of these hold:
- **The tool isn't an MCP tool.** Codex gives MCP tools names with a double underscore (`server__tool` or `mcp__server__tool`). Their output schemas belong to whoever wrote the tool, which is where an accidental match could happen.
- **The object has exactly two keys, `output` and `metadata`.** Anything with extra keys stays as it is.

**Why not Codex's suggested allowlist of shell tool names:** Sarvam wraps every built-in tool's result in this envelope, `write_file` included. A shell-only list would leave those results as raw JSON.

**New tests:**
- A `write_file` envelope is unwrapped.
- An MCP tool returning the exact envelope shape is left unchanged. I removed the guard and confirmed this test fails without it.
- An object with an extra key is left unchanged.

**Checks:**
- The real Sarvam rollout still converts correctly: `write_file` comes out as success with exit code 0, and the failing command as an error with exit code 1.
- Lint is clean.
- The transcript, checkpoint and agent package tests pass.
- The README now describes both conditions.

I'll report when the checks and trail findings come back.
